summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies, including the orders on sex classification in documents and federal facilities (EO 14168), gender-affirming care funding (EO 14187) and athletic participation (EO 14201), the last of which is paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all US identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth, new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents, and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked, with some stranded abroad, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs; Lambda Legal and the Human Rights Campaign document how name and gender changes now interact with federal records. A trans visitor holding US documents faces that mismatch at Pago Pago, where screening follows US federal procedure.

The same January 2025 order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities used in accordance with their gender identity. The territory's hospital is federally funded, and the orders halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reach it, so a trans visitor who needs emergency or inpatient care may be placed in a ward or room corresponding to sex assigned at birth, or be separated from care that was previously funded.

Discrimination on the basis of gender identity in territory employment has produced federal enforcement. In September 2023 the US Department of Justice secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, and in June 2023 a federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen, one of the documented trans-specific violence records for the territory.

Marriage recognition remains contested on the ground. The Fono Senate voted down a bill in March 2003 that would have outlawed same-sex marriage, after the House judiciary committee recommended it be killed. In January 2016 the newly confirmed District Court judge Fiti Alexander Sunia told the Senate he had not read Obergefell and that the district court did not deal with the ruling, and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws changed. As of July 2024 an on-island constitutional survey by Professor Daniel Hall was still testing whether the territory's same-sex marriage ban would survive a Fourteenth Amendment challenge, indicating the local ban is treated as operative. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that Obergefell does apply and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied; no same-sex couple has applied for a licence to date, and the litigation path runs through the High Court of American Samoa against the Territorial Registrar and then the US Department of the Interior.

Social climate differs from the legal posture. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, is described in university research as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, and the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association on an explicitly cultural-pride footing. Contemporary commentary reports homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture while noting that reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, so visible nonconformity attracts comment more readily than official sanction.
tangentialFactors:
Other US territories moved to apply the 2015 federal marriage ruling while American Samoa's attorney general said in 2015 that applicability was still under review; Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands had resolved the question, and no licence applications had been made in American Samoa at that point.

A 2009 travel column contrasts the territory with what it calls homophobia in Fiji, and records that fa'afafine locals openly courted Western visitors; the same source notes the fa'amatai chiefly system structures social life in both Samoan nations, and that Pago Pago hotels skew business rather than leisure travel. Local artist Dan Taulapapa McMullin has called the Samoan islands the homeland of fa'afafine culture.

At the 2003 committee hearing on the marriage ban bill, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine did not seek marriages with other men, describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech and citing Christian upbringing. The bill's sponsor, Representative Sua Carl Schuster, introduced it to preempt the marriage litigation then unfolding in US states.

The 2024 survey by Dr Daniel Hall, a constitutional and comparative law professor at Miami University, tests not only constitutional durability but also whether the territory's collectivistic orientation and polychronic relationship to time bear on how such a challenge would be argued locally.
localsOnly:
Residents are covered by the terms of the September 2023 Department of Justice settlement with the American Samoa Government on harassment of a transgender employee, and by the litigation that produced the June 2023 hostile-work-environment finding against the territorial government; these are resident-facing employment protections and complaint routes rather than visitor entitlements.

Local gender-nonconforming residents organise through the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, founded in 2010 from the merger of the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, with fa'afafine identity framed as cultural reclamation rather than a Western import.

The fa'amatai chiefly system and church affiliation shape everyday expectations of dress and conduct for residents of all orientations, and reserved public behaviour is the local norm.

Resident couples seeking a marriage licence apply through the Territorial Registrar; a 2026 analysis by attorneys practising locally holds that the registrar must issue a certificate to a same-sex couple, and maps the challenge route through the High Court of American Samoa and then the US Department of Interior, though no couple has applied.

Fiti Alexander Sunia, confirmed unanimously as District Court judge in January 2016, remains the named judicial officer on record regarding performance of same-sex weddings absent a change in local law.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether Obergefell is operative in American Samoa in practice is asserted in both directions by sourced material, a 2016 judicial statement and a 2026 law review conclusion, and no case has tested it; the territory's own marriage statute and its constitutional durability after the July 2024 survey are not settled in the sources.

Not sourced: whether the territory's hospital has actually altered ward assignment or care-funding practice since the January 2025 orders, and whether any trans visitor has been refused entry, detained or referred at Pago Pago on document grounds.

Unverified in the inventory: the current status of the ACLU suit against the State Department, the outcome of the Lambda Legal guidance as litigation proceeds, and the precise scope of the SWS25 visa restriction as applied to arrivals in this territory.

Open: whether the September 2023 DOJ settlement terms have been implemented, and whether any hate-crime or employment complaint by a trans person has been filed since February 2023.
